canard

kuh-NARD · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Canard is an unfounded rumor or story; a lie repeated as if true.

The rumor that the school was closing for good turned out to be nothing more than a canard started by a disgruntled parent online.

Example

The story that eating late at night causes weight gain by itself has been repeated for decades, but nutritionists have shown it's really just a canard -- what matters is overall calories, not the clock.

A claim that gets repeated so often people assume it's true, even though it isn't, is exactly what a canard is.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

falsehood: A falsehood is any single statement that is not true, from a small fib to a big lie. A canard is a falsehood with a career: an untrue story that has been repeated so often people treat it as common knowledge.

fabrication: A fabrication is a story someone deliberately made up — the word points at the inventing itself. A canard points at the circulation: it is the false claim that keeps spreading because people repeat it as true, long after anyone remembers who invented it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

fact: something known to be true

truth: the actual state of things

Where it sits · how deliberately the falsehood is built

rumor → canard → hoax

rumor vs. canard: A rumor is less deliberately built than a canard: a rumor just drifts by word of mouth, with nobody sure where it started, while a canard is a definite false story that keeps being repeated as if it were established fact.

hoax vs. canard: A hoax is stronger than a canard: a canard is a false story passed along as true, while a hoax goes further -- an elaborate, staged deception complete with fake press releases and photographs.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — canard: duck (French)

Put it together: Canard is simply the French word for 'duck.' The false-story meaning is thought to come from an old French idiom about half-selling a duck -- an old expression for fooling someone -- and the word crossed into English still carrying that sense of a fabricated tale.

Use the root in a new word: duck: Canard is simply French for 'duck' -- the false-story meaning may trace back to an old idiom about half-selling a duck, a phrase once used to describe fooling someone.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Canard is a somewhat formal, almost journalistic word for a persistent false story -- it works well for a repeated myth or rumor, but sounds odd for a single small lie.
